hints: Focus on linking the measured gas volume to moles, since $M_r$ comes from mass divided by moles.
Start by finding $n$ with $pV = nRT$, using $p = 1.013 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}$, $V = 4.50 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}^3$ and $T = 373 \text{ K}$.
Divide $0.175 \text{ g}$ by your tiny mole value to get mass per mole, and see which value near 120 it matches.
walkthrough:
**Spot this as an ideal gas moles question**

Think of the vapour as an ideal gas. That means we can find moles from pressure, volume and temperature.

We will use:
$$pV = nRT$$

**Convert temperature to kelvin**

Never use Celsius in $pV = nRT$. Always add 273.

$$T = 100 + 273 = 373 \text{ K}$$

**Calculate moles of vapour**

Rearrange to $n = pV / RT$ and put in SI units. Volume is already in $\text{m}^3$ and pressure in $\text{Pa}$, so no conversion is needed.

$$n = \frac{(1.013 \times 10^5)(4.50 \times 10^{-5})}{8.31 \times 373}$$
$$n = \frac{4.5585}{3099.6} \approx 1.47 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$

**Convert mass and moles to $M_r$**

Relative molecular mass is mass of one mole. So divide the given mass by the moles you found.

$$M_r = \frac{m}{n} = \frac{0.175}{1.47 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 119$$

options.A: Incorrect. 31.9 comes from using $T = 100 \text{ K}$ instead of $373 \text{ K}$. Using Celsius directly makes $RT$ far too small, so $n$ looks far too large and $M_r = m/n$ looks far too small.
options.B: Incorrect. 87.1 comes from using $T = 273 \text{ K}$ (0 C) instead of $373 \text{ K}$ (100 C). This is the classic STP temperature trap. A lower T gives a larger $n$ and therefore a smaller $M_r$.
options.C: Correct. Using $n = pV/RT$ with correct SI units and $T = 373 \text{ K}$ gives $n \approx 1.47 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$. Then $M_r = 0.175 / n \approx 119$, which is the molar mass of the liquid.
options.D: Incorrect. 127 is a little higher than the true value. It typically comes from rounding $n$ down too early or a small slip in $pV/RT$, giving too few moles and so $m/n$ is pushed too high.
